```{r setup, include=FALSE}

template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function (arg0_path) {
  lines <- readLines(arg0_path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  lines <- sub("^\\s*//.*$", "", lines)
  lines <- sub("(?<!:)//.*$", "", lines, perl = TRUE)
  txt <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  txt <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", txt, perl = TRUE)
  txt <- gsub(",(\\s*[}\\]])", "\\1", txt, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(txt, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("korea_under_japanese_occupation.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("korea_under_japanese_occupation_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("korea_under_japanese_occupation_source_ledger.json5")

reg_names <- c(
  gyeonggi_13do = "Gyeonggi",
  north_chungcheong_13do = "North Chungcheong",
  south_chungcheong_13do = "South Chungcheong",
  north_jeolla_13do = "North Jeolla",
  south_jeolla_13do = "South Jeolla and Jeju",

  south_gyeongsang_13do = "South Gyeongsang",
  gangwon_13do = "Gangwon",
  hwanghae_13do = "Hwanghae",
  south_pyongan_13do = "South Pyongan",

  south_hamgyong_13do = "South Hamgyong",

)
```

# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 581 urban, administrative, industrial and port settlements active across Korea between 1905AD and 1945AD (covering 226.901 km² across thirteen provincial territories). Synthesising colonial census gazetteers (*Chōsen Sōtokufu Tōkei Nenpō*), the quinquennial census series (1925AD, 1930AD, 1935AD, 1940AD, 1944AD), historical cadastres, and post-liberation municipal registers [@KOSIS2021Census; @SBJ2021Census; @Kwon1977Demography; @NSTAC2026SSDSE], the gazetteer encompasses every primary administrative and economic node: the capital metropolis of Keijo (Seoul, 935k), provincial capitals, 12 designated colonial municipalities (*bu*), 218 unified county seats (*gun*), open treaty ports (*kaehangjang*), railway junctions, and northern heavy chemical and metallurgical hubs. Across the 581 catalogued entries, the dataset documents 4.941 settlement-year population observations spanning 1905AD to 1945AD (averaging 8,00 observations per centre). At peak colonial urbanisation, the leading urban centres were Seoul (935k), Pyongyang (310k), Busan (281k), Incheon (215k), Daegu (205k), Chongjin (198k), Hamhung (118k), Sinuiju (117k), Wonsan (111k), Gwangju (85k), Haeju (82k), Kaesong (81k), Nampo (81k), Jeonju (77k) and Daejeon (75k). Alongside the 581 catalogued settlements, the regional source ledger records 3 excluded candidate entries (Gwangju duplicate alias, Goseong duplicate alias and Ulleung outside study bounds) out of 584 total evaluated candidates.

# Background

Urbanisation in colonial Korea was structured by the intersection of traditional administrative hierarchies and modern Japanese transport and industrial infrastructure [@Kwon1977Demography; @KOSIS2021Census; @Kong1997Conclusion]. Prior to annexation, Korean urban centres functioned primarily as walled county administrative seats (*eupchi*) and market towns where local magistrates collected grain taxes and supervised rural markets [@KwonShin1977Joseon; @Cha2009LivingStandards].

Under the Government-General of Chosen, the peninsular urban network was restructured into three functional tiers [@KOSIS2021Census; @NSTAC2026SSDSE]. First, twelve designated municipal prefectures (*bu*) concentrated colonial administrative departments, commercial banks, Japanese trading firms, and manufacturing operations, led by Seoul, Busan, Pyongyang, Incheon and Daegu [@KOSIS2021Census]. Second, the expansion of the trunk railway grid created thriving junction towns such as Daejeon, Iri (Iksan) and Suncheon, which eclipsed older neighbouring county seats in trade volume and population [@Xia2024Impact; @Dyrting2024Estimating]. Third, northern industrialisation from the late 1920s transformed fishing villages and mining stations into sprawling heavy industrial cities, notably the chemical complexes at Hamhung and Hungnam, the metallurgical port of Chongjin, and the border timber and chemical centre at Sinuiju [@EberstadtBanister1992; @Spoorenberg2012DPRK].

# Methodology

Settlement records were constructed by harmonising the administrative time-series of the Government-General of Chosen with the 1925AD to 1944AD quinquennial censuses, municipal cadastral surveys, and post-colonial municipal registries [@KOSIS2021Census; @SBJ2021Census; @NSTAC2026SSDSE]. All 581 catalogued settlements carry verified historical coordinates and assign to one of the thirteen provincial masks.

In the regional source ledger, 3 candidate records were excluded during deduplication and bounds verification [@KOSIS2021Census]. These exclusions comprised:
1. Gwangju (South Korea), excluded as a duplicate alias of canonical Gwangju in South Jeolla to avoid confounding with Gwangju county in Gyeonggi.
2. Goseong (South Korea), excluded as a duplicate alias of canonical Goseong in South Gyeongsang to prevent overlap with Goseong county in Gangwon.
3. Ulleung (South Korea), situated in the Sea of Japan beyond the contiguous peninsular masking boundaries.

# Testing and Validation

Ledger reconciliation confirms 581 included settlements and 3 excluded candidate entries (584 total evaluated entities, with zero unaccounted records). All 581 settlements carry geographic coordinates and population time-series for the colonial benchmarks. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} displays the rank-size distribution and the leading urban centres of the peninsula.

# Results

## Top 45 Settlements by Peak Population

Table \ref{tab:top45-korea} presents the top 45 settlements in the gazetteer ordered by peak documented population, illustrating the dominance of the capital metropolis, the primary railway and ferry terminus at Busan, and the industrial centers of the north.

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function(x) gsub("[.]", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))

get_pop_str <- function(e, y) {
  v <- e[["population"]][[y]]
  if (is.null(v)) return("-")
  viscount_fmt_pop(v)
}

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function(e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e[["population"]]))
  pks <- as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))
  pk_y <- names(e[["population"]])[which.max(pks)]
  pk_v <- max(pks)
  reg_label <- if (e[["region_id"]] %in% names(reg_names)) reg_names[[e[["region_id"]]]] else e[["region_id"]]
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e[["name"]],
    Province = reg_label,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[2]])),
    Span = paste0(min(yrs), "-", max(yrs), "AD"),
    P1905 = get_pop_str(e, "1905"),
    P1925 = get_pop_str(e, "1925"),
    P1940 = get_pop_str(e, "1940"),
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", pk_y, "AD)"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 settlements in Korea ordered by peak documented population (581 total sites).",
  c("Settlement", "Province", "Lat, Lon", "Span", "1905AD", "1925AD", "1940AD", "Peak (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-korea", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 32L)
)
```

## Sub-Regional Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-korea} summarises the distribution of settlements across all thirteen provincial territories alongside their leading urban centres. Gyeonggi leads all territories with 82 catalogued settlements, followed by Gangwon (66), North Gyeongsang (60), North Pyongan (60), Hwanghae (51), South Gyeongsang (50), and South Chungcheong (43). Table \ref{tab:excluded-korea} details the 3 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger.

```{r tab-regsum, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)

sum_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(e[["region_id"]], rk), sett_data)
  max_nm <- "-"
  if (length(sub_e) > 0) {
    pks <- vapply(sub_e, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
    idx_m <- which.max(pks)
    max_nm <- paste0(sub_e[[idx_m]][["name"]], " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ")")
  }
  reg_short <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[rk]]$name)
  data.frame(
    Territory = gsub("&", "and", reg_short, fixed = TRUE),
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_e)),
    Lead = max_nm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  "Settlement counts and leading urban centres across the thirteen Korean provincial territories (581 total sites).",
  c("Territory", "Catalogued Sites", "Leading Centre (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:regsum-korea", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 20L)
)
```

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function(c) identical(c[["status"]], "excluded"), ledger_data[["candidates"]])

exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list, function(c) {
  just <- as.character(c[["justification"]])
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c[["name"]],
    Territory = c[["country"]],
    Classification = c[["reason"]],
    Consolidation_Justification = just,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "Excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger, consolidated into canonical settlements.",
  c("Candidate", "Territory", "Classification", "Consolidation Justification"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-korea", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Limitations

Two spatial factors affect urban population aggregation in this gazetteer. First, municipal boundary revisions expanded the legal administrative territory (*bu-yeok*) of major cities during the late colonial period. Most notably, Keijo (Seoul) underwent substantial territorial annexations in April 1936 and October 1940, incorporating suburban industrial districts in Yeongdeungpo, Mapo, Yongsan and Dongdaemun from surrounding Gyeonggi-do county districts. These administrative enlargements are tracked through unified municipal totals to capture contiguous metropolitan agglomerations rather than artificial administrative ruptures [@Kwon1977Demography; @KOSIS2021Census]. Second, in rapidly expanding northern mining and chemical districts such as Hungnam, Musan and Kaechon, large numbers of unmarried male construction and factory labourers lived in factory dormitories and temporary worker barracks that were partially under-enumerated during regular de jure municipal surveys [@EberstadtBanister1992; @Spoorenberg2012DPRK].
